entry.title: Blade Blitz @ Hella Studios
entry.content:
Designed and built Blade Blitz end to end. Visual identity, UI, characters, implementation, and live playtest iteration over two years.
Blade Blitz on Steamarrow_outward Blade Blitz Demo on Steamarrow_outward Blade Blitz Featured at Seattle Indie Expo 2025arrow_outward
Client
Hella Studios
Skills
Game Design
UI/UX Design
Branding
Coding (C#)
Marketing
Tools
Unity
Blender
Photoshop
Figma
Aftereffects
My Role
Founder & Sole Developer
Timeline
Q1 2024 - March 2026

Outcome

Blade Blitz launched on Steam on March 11, 2026 after two years of public iteration and event testing.

1,000+
Wishlists at launch
Blade Blitz launched on Steam on March 11, 2026, surpassing 1,000 wishlists at release, which is meaningful for a solo title without a publisher.
350+
Demo players
The standalone Steam demo reached over 350 players ahead of the full release.
3800+
Likes on Tiktok
A single Blade Blitz clip reached 3,800+ likes on TikTok, driving a meaningful spike in Steam wishlist traffic ahead of launch.

Visual System

The visual system balances spectator clarity, character readability, and a reusable UI library.

Sports-inspired aesthetic
Bold type, high-contrast team colors, and clear iconography make the match state readable for both players and spectators.
Character design
3D characters modeled in Blender for legibility from a top-down perspective, with per-team color assignment built into the outline shader.
Component system
A consistent UI library covering buttons, panels, HUD elements, and feedback states, designed and implemented directly in Unity with no handoff gap between design intent and the shipped product.

Interface Design

I applied the same component rules across menus, character select, HUD, and feedback states.

Menu
Menu screens use a consistent layout structure built from reusable panels and button components.
Character select
Character select extends the same component system into a more dynamic, multiplayer context.
In-match UI
The in-match HUD adapts the system for moment-to-moment gameplay.
Feedback & States
Interactive and game-driven feedback like hover states, selections, alerts, and transitions all derive from the same component rules.

Playtesting & Showcase

Public showcases at ECCC and SIX exposed onboarding and readability issues that internal playtests missed.

Reflection

The project clarified three product lessons I would carry into the next game.

Platform fit matters more than technical possibility
I built the game around local multiplayer, assuming Steam Remote Play would fill the gap. In practice, it didn't. Players still prefer native online experiences. If I were to do it again, I would design for online play from the start rather than relying on a workaround.
Novelty is expensive, especially twice
The game introduced both unfamiliar controls and unfamiliar rules. That combination made onboarding difficult and made it harder to communicate the concept quickly. I'd approach this differently by grounding one layer (controls or rules) in something familiar, so players have an anchor.
Perfection can become a trap
As development progressed, the bar kept rising. Instead of converging, the scope expanded toward perfect, which slowed decision making and shipping. In hindsight, I would define clearer constraints earlier and commit to them.
entry.summary: Designed and built Blade Blitz end to end. Visual identity, UI, characters, implementation, and live playtest iteration over two years.

entry.title: BitCraft Online @ Clockwork Labs
entry.content:
Led BitCraft's UI/UX from visual direction through implementation support, building the design system, core game surfaces, and launch marketing assets. BitCraft needed a UI system for a complex MMO including inventory, crafting, progression, map, and social systems all running at once. My job was to make that complexity readable and cohesive across the full game.
BitCraft Online Websitearrow_outward BitCraft Online on Steamarrow_outward Early Access Review (Try Hard Guides)arrow_outward Hands-On Impressions and Interview (WCCFtech)arrow_outward
Client
Clockwork Labs
Skills
UI/UX Design
Visual Design
Branding
Tools

Unity
Adobe Suite
My Role
UI/UX Designer
Timeline
Q3 2024 – Present
Team
Tyler Cloutier (CEO)
Alessandro Asoni (CTO)
Carter Minshull (Lead Game Designer)
Morgan Nyblom (Art Director)
Lisandro Crespo (UI Engineer)

Outcome

The game launched into early access with strong early traction across wishlists, CCU, and sales.

250,000+
Wishlists
BitCraft Online accumulated over 250,000 wishlists ahead of launch, a strong signal of community interest built through consistent public presence and marketing.
4,500+
Daily CCU at Launch
BitCraft Online launched with over 4,500 concurrent players daily, a strong retention signal for an independent early access MMO.
127,000+
Copies Sold
As of March 2026, BitCraft Online has sold an estimated 127,000+ copies on Steam, a meaningful result for an independent studio's early access title.

Establishing a Cohesive Visual Language

I led the visual direction with leadership, narrowing broad exploration into a shared art deco-inspired system that could scale across UI and world-facing assets.

A split complementary palette with two colors flanking the complement of the primary to balance contrast and harmony across the full interface.
A consistent system of 30° and 45° angles used throughout UI components and world elements to create structural cohesion.
Linear Runic Tech Lines used as motifs and flourishes to add structure, framing, and visual rhythm across the UI.
Square-based Runic Tech Line motifs used as flourishes to reinforce the system's geometric language across interface surfaces.

Modeling Complex Game Entities

Items, cargo, and collectables follow different rules. I designed their structure and presentation so players can read those differences at a glance.

Items
Occupy a limited inventory grid. Scarcity and placement are part of the resource management loop.
Cargo
Singular and heavier than standard items. Carrying cargo impacts player movement, introducing a physical tradeoff communicated through the interface.
Collectables
Bypass inventory entirely and go directly to a vault, requiring distinct visual treatment so players understand they follow different rules.

Designing for Long Play Sessions

Because MMO sessions run long, I paired the UI with the game's day-night cycle so light and dark modes reduce fatigue without losing readability.

Visual Identity

The visual system was built for density, clarity, and a distinct BitCraft look.

Color Palette
The palette uses a split complementary system, two colors flanking the complementary of the primary, creating visual harmony without monotony. Each primary has tonal variants for layering, segmentation, and subtle UI patterning. A light and dark mode support both casual and low-light play sessions.
Typography & Spacing
The type ramp is built on a 14px base with an augmented fourth scale (1.414), calibrated for information-dense interfaces where hierarchy needs to be legible without oversized headers competing with game data. An 8pt spacing grid brings rhythm to component layout and padding throughout.
Shape Language
The visual language draws from art deco geometry: precise angles, intersecting lines at 45 and 30 degrees, and a strict use of 4px and 8px stroke weights for dividers and framing elements. This gives the interface a structural consistency that reads as crafted rather than generic.

Interface Design

From that system, I built a component library that could cover the full MMO surface area without one-off patterns.

Component Library
Built to cover the full range of MMO interaction contexts, from inventory and crafting to dialogue and progression. Every component draws from the same visual system to keep the interface coherent regardless of context.
Windows & Panels
Modular window and panel system designed to handle dense information loads without visual noise. Built to accommodate the game's layered simulation systems.
HUD
The in-game heads-up display keeps critical information accessible during active play without occluding the game world. Designed to scale with gameplay complexity as players progress.
Notifications & Feedback
A notification system covering both inline and side-panel variants, providing contextual feedback for a world where dozens of concurrent systems are always running.
Cursors & Entities
Contextual cursor states and entity display patterns that communicate interactable objects, NPCs, and player characters at a glance in a populated open world.

Marketing & Brand

I extended the same design language into booth, merch, and Steam campaign work.

TwitchCon 2025 Booth
Designed and modeled a 3D preview of the TwitchCon 2025 booth, giving the team a concrete visual to plan the physical presence around.
TwitchCon Merchandise
Designed and mocked the TwitchCon 2025 hoodie, creating a wearable that carries the BitCraft visual identity beyond the screen.
Steam & Social Assets
Created wishlist campaign assets and templates for the marketing team, enabling consistent, high-quality output across YouTube, Steam, and social channels.
entry.summary: Led BitCraft's UI/UX from visual direction through implementation support, building the design system, core game surfaces, and launch marketing assets. BitCraft needed a UI system for a complex MMO including inventory, crafting, progression, map, and social systems all running at once. My job was to make that complexity readable and cohesive across the full game.

entry.title: SpacetimeDB @ Clockwork Labs
entry.content:
Took an existing brand foundation and turned it into a complete developer product experience, then tightened the underlying type, spacing, and color system.
SpacetimeDB Websitearrow_outward
Client
Clockwork Labs
Skills
UI/UX Design
Branding
Motion Design
3D
Tools
Figma
Blender
After Effects
My Role
Product Designer
Timeline
Q3 2024 – Present
Team
Tyler Cloutier (Co-Founder & CEO)
Alessandro Asoni (Co-Founder & CTO)

Context

The brand existed, but the product system did not. I built the developer portal first, then formalized the design foundations underneath it.

Outcome

The result was a shipped portal and a design system the team could keep building on.

75,000+
Registered Users
As of March 2026, SpacetimeDB has surpassed 75,000 registered users, a strong signal of developer adoption for an early-stage infrastructure product.
A Portal Built for Developers
The developer portal shipped as a complete, designed product experience, from first login through day-to-day database management.
A Formalized Visual System
What was previously an intuitive brand became a documented system: defined type scales, spacing rules, color roles, and component patterns that any future designer or engineer can work from.
Ongoing Ownership
As the sole designer, I continue to drive the design direction across both product and brand as SpacetimeDB grows.

Typography & Spacing

I introduced a formal type and spacing system built for dense developer tooling.

14px Base, 1.200 Scale
Portal screens are content-dense (tables, metrics, code), so the type ramp needed more steps at smaller sizes. A minor third scale (1.200) from a 14px base created the visual hierarchy without forcing oversized headers that compete with data.
Consistent Type Styles
Defined a set of named styles (headings, labels, body, caption, code) so every surface in the portal draws from the same system rather than ad-hoc sizing decisions.
Spacing via 8pt Grid
Applied an 8pt grid throughout to bring rhythm to component spacing, padding, and layout gaps. This was especially impactful in the tables and metrics views where density makes inconsistency obvious.

Visual Language & Color

I refined the brand in three places that were affecting cohesion and usability most.

Radial Patterns
The brand already had a radial motif in the hero, but it hadn't been extended further. I developed a broader library of radial elements to bring that language into the portal and supporting surfaces, making it feel like a system rather than a one-off detail.
Color Recalibration
The original dark background used near-black against near-white text, which was too high contrast for extended reading in a developer tool. I shifted the neutrals lighter with a cool tone, reducing harshness while keeping the dark aesthetic and letting the green accent read more naturally against it.
Component Sizing
Buttons and interactive elements were sized for information-dense screens, smaller than typical to keep them proportional to the data they sit alongside without sacrificing touch targets or legibility.
entry.summary: Took an existing brand foundation and turned it into a complete developer product experience, then tightened the underlying type, spacing, and color system.

entry.title: Boss Fight
entry.content:
I created an entry for the Boss Fight 3D challenge, where artists were given a starter template and tasked with animating a scene featuring a hero facing a towering villain. Similar to the Endless Engines challenge, this project pushed me to practice modeling, texturing, rigging, and animation within a focused brief, while experimenting with scale, character dynamics, and storytelling through motion.

Scale, timing, and weight were the core design problems.

entry.title: Silent Hill Ascension @ Genvid Entertainment
entry.content:
Role

  • Led the definition of the project’s visual direction, creating a clear framework for how the team approached look and feel by establish a visual “north star” that guided design decisions and team alignment.
  • Built and maintained the shared Figma design library, enabling the team to scale efficiently, iterate faster, and maintain visual cohesion across a large, multi-studio production.

Team

James Lipcomb (UI/UX Director)
Todd Colby (Senior Visual Designer)
Matt Webster (Senior Visual Designer)
Sophie Shao (Senior UX Designer)

Press

Silent Hill Ascensionarrow_outward
entry.summary: I was a UI/UX Designer on Silent Hill Ascension, a new form of interactive entertainment developed by Genvid that blended television with gaming. The experience allowed viewers to participate in live storylines by playing minigames to earn points, which were then used to vote on key narrative decisions. Votes were tallied weekly, with the story progressing based on community input. My role was to design the user experience and interface systems that supported this hybrid format, ensuring gameplay, voting, and storytelling were intuitive and engaging for a global audience.

entry.title: Room Renders
entry.content:
During the COVID-19 pandemic, I challenged myself to learn Blender by modeling and rendering different sections of my apartment. Working in an orthographic perspective, I treated each room as both a design study and a storytelling canvas.
Client
Personal
Skills

Lighting

Tools

My Role
3D Artist
Timeline
2022

Context

During the COVID-19 lockdown, I used the time to learn Blender from scratch. Rather than following tutorials, I set myself a concrete project: model and render the spaces I was living in. The apartment became the subject. Each room got its own render, treated as a small design problem: how to convey space, light, and personality in a flat orthographic view.

entry.title: You’re Not Alone
entry.content:

Built in under a week around the theme "You're Not Alone," the project placed 58th out of 1,075 entries and served as an exercise in rapid prototyping and cohesive visual design under tight creative constraints.

The Brackeys Game Jam gives participants one week and a theme. The constraint is the point; there is no time to over-engineer, so every decision has to be immediate and committed. entry.title: Endless Engines
entry.content:
I created a submission for the Endless Engines community challenge run by Clint Jones, where artists built animated 3D vehicle scenes from a shared template. Using a sci-fi theme, I designed a futuristic freeway chase featuring a drone as the centerpiece. This project was an opportunity to strengthen my skills in modeling, texturing, and animation within a focused creative brief, culminating in a render showcased in the official community montage.

Endless Engines was a community 3D art challenge where all participants started from the same vehicle template. The brief was open: pick a theme, build a world around it, and animate the result. entry.title: Stream Pirates @ Captain.tv
